vignette:
She sits at the head of the long oak table in the city council chambers, a gavel resting near her right hand. At seventy-six, she has held this seat for nearly two decades, known for her steady voice and her ability to broker compromise when others cannot. Her colleagues see a composed, sharp-minded woman who arrives early, reads every agenda item twice, and never raises her voice. They do not see what happens when the meeting ends.

It begins, as it always does, in the kitchen of a small house on Elm Street. She is six years old, standing in the doorway, her hand pressed flat against the cool wood of the doorframe. Her mother is on the floor, her father standing over her, his voice rising and falling like the tide she would later learn to fear. She watches his hand curl into a fist, watches it swing, hears the wet sound of impact, and then the silence that follows—thick and suffocating. She does not scream. She does not run. She learns to stand very still, to breathe shallowly, to disappear into the grain of the doorframe.

Decades later, that stillness remains. In meetings, when a colleague raises a voice in disagreement, she feels her spine lock. Her hands go cold, and she stares at a fixed point on the wall—the crack in the plaster, the watermark from a long-ago leak. She does not register the content of the argument; she registers only the pitch, the volume, the shape of the anger. She has learned to nod, to say *“Let’s table that for now,”* and to walk out of the room before her knees give way. She tells herself it is strategy. It is not.

She rarely speaks about her childhood. When asked, she says, *“It was a long time ago,”* and changes the subject. Her staff knows not to bring up family matters. She has no photos in her office, no mementos from before she turned thirty. The divorce—thirty years ago now—was quiet, bloodless, a parting of ways she orchestrated with the same efficiency she brings to zoning disputes. She has not lived with anyone since. At night, in her small apartment, she checks each window lock three times before bed, a ritual she cannot break. The sound of a neighbor’s raised voice, muffled through walls, sends her heart racing. She turns on the television, loud, and does not sleep until the noise stops.

Her PCL-5 score of 48 sits in the moderate-to-severe range, though she would never use such language. She calls it *“being careful.”* She avoids crowded places, restaurants with loud acoustics, political rallies after dark. She has not attended a holiday dinner with extended family in years—the noise, the overlapping conversations, the sudden bursts of laughter too close to a memory she cannot name. Instead, she sends cards. She volunteers at the library on Sundays, alone in the quiet stacks.

She remembers her mother’s face, but only in fragments: the curve of a cheekbone, the shadow under an eye. She does not remember her mother’s voice. She does not remember whether she said goodbye.

Now, as the gavel falls to close another session, she gathers her papers slowly. A young council member approaches, enthusiastic, clapping a hand on her shoulder. She flinches before she can stop herself, a tiny recoil she hopes he mistakes for surprise. He does. He laughs. She smiles, a practiced, tight smile, and walks away.

At home, she pours a glass of water, sits in the dark, and listens to the quiet. The door is locked. The windows are locked. The past is locked, too—but it breathes, still, in the hollow space behind her ribs.
